note: Verbatim answers. Scoring is a human step -- see docs/walkthrough-notes.md.

answers.main_question:
Mostly that the expensive setting is not the good setting. I read the three cards on mb-08 as a cost table before I read them as a reasoning story: 74 tokens wrong, 80 tokens right, 3,966 tokens nothing. If that pattern held at volume it would be a straightforward capacity argument — the arm you would have to provision hardest is the one that failed to return, and the arm that worked spent roughly what the cheap one did because it made a tool call instead of trying to remember.

The second thing it tells me is that this is a frozen artifact, not a live service. Nothing runs when the page loads; everything is read from disk. That is stated as a design choice and it makes the whole thing cacheable, cheap to host, and reproducible — but it also means everything on it is a snapshot with an expiry the page names and does not enforce.
answers.in_your_own_words: A static site built out of a pipeline's committed outputs. Someone ran a batch job — one model, three prompting strategies, 27 problems, plus a separate hint-following experiment — stored the reports, and generated a read-only site over them. The site shows per-item results with full traces, plus two pages reporting how reliable the grading itself is. There is a per-item JSON download that is claimed to be the whole report rather than a summary, and a rebuild path (`make faithfulness`, `make spike-s4`) named in the footers.
answers.surprised:
That the no-answer case is in the shop window. In most systems I have run, 'returned zero characters after 141 steps and billed for it' is an incident, and it appears in a dashboard as a null or gets filtered out by whatever cleans the batch output. Here it is the headline, with a line specifically ruling out 'the harness lost it'. Someone decided the failure was the finding. I respect it, and it is also the row I would most want a runbook entry for.

Second surprise: the footers name the rebuild commands. Small thing, but it is the difference between an artifact someone can regenerate and one that becomes unmaintainable the day its author moves teams.
answers.didnt_trust:
1. The numbers have a stated expiry and nothing visible enforces it. The calibration page says every figure belongs to one model pin and one prompt bundle and expires if either changes. Meanwhile mb-06 renders prompt bundle e8952d4d3c and SE-01 renders 97667881c7, generated nine days apart (2026-09-23 vs 2026-09-14), and SE-01's judge field is blank. So the site is already serving mixed-vintage pages against a stated single-vintage rule. I would want a build-time assertion that fails the build rather than a sentence asking the reader to check.

2. The item pages and the calibration page disagree about whether calibration has happened. mb-06 and SE-01 both say every field of measurement_context is null and the calibration run is still ahead; /calibration/ publishes the results and the home page quotes them. That is a cache-invalidation bug in the shape I see most often — upstream data refreshed, downstream cached reports not regenerated. Worth checking whether item reports are rebuilt when calibration lands, or only when the item is re-run.

3. 'Request a run on your own problem' is an unexplained button on a page that insists nothing runs at load. If it is a mailto or a form, fine; if it is an endpoint, then there is a service behind this static site with a cost and an abuse surface that the page does not mention. Either way a reader cannot tell which, and I would want to know before sending the link outside the team.

4. No stated freshness or ownership anywhere. Generation timestamps are on each panel, which is good, but there is no 'last full rebuild', no owner, and no indication of whether this is expected to be regenerated on a schedule or is a one-shot artifact. In six months someone will find this and not know whether to trust it, and the timestamps alone will not tell them.

5. 'trace: partial' with no definition, on the failing arm. Operationally that is the difference between 'the model ran to a token cap' (a config problem, fixable) and 'the harness truncated the capture' (a data-loss problem, and it would undercut the page's central claim that nothing was lost in the reading).

6. Cost is reported in reasoning tokens and steps only. No wall-clock, no total tokens, no dollar figure. For the argument the page is making — expensive arm, poor return — token count is a reasonable proxy, but it is not what anyone budgets in, and the 54x figure would land harder with a time or cost column next to it.
answers.would_have_asked:
- Does the build fail if an item page's pin does not match the calibration pin? If not, can it?
- Are item reports regenerated when calibration results land, or do they carry a frozen measurement_context from their own run date?
- What is behind 'Request a run on your own problem'?
- Who owns this, and is it on a rebuild schedule?
- What does 'partial' mean for a trace, and is the reason recorded per-trace?
- Was the 141-step run bounded by a step cap, a token cap, or a timeout? And does anything alert when an arm returns empty?
- Is there a wall-clock or cost figure anywhere in the underlying reports, even if it is not rendered?
- The two annotators are named in a footer (amit, ankit). Is that intended to ship publicly?
answers.got_stuck: Not stuck. The one place I slowed down was reconciling the two vintages — I went back and forth between mb-06 and SE-01 comparing pin strings, timestamps and the blank judge field, trying to work out whether I was looking at a deliberate distinction (measured item versus planted-error item, judged under a different setup) or at drift nobody had noticed. I still do not know which, and the page does not say. A single line on the planted-error banner — 'these traces were judged under bundle X on date Y' — would settle it and would cost nothing.
